title: Demonstrate an understanding of professional values and ethics

lessons.title: What professional values are and where they come from
lessons.html:
Values in professional work

Values are the beliefs about what is right, important and worth protecting that guide how we act. Professional values are the shared standards expected of people in a particular occupation, such as an extension practitioner, an animal health technician or a farm manager. Typical examples are honesty, integrity, competence, respect for clients, fairness, confidentiality, accountability and care for animals and the environment.

Sources of values

  • Personal and family background: upbringing, religion, culture and community, for example ubuntu, the idea that a person is a person through other people.
  • Society and the Constitution: the Bill of Rights sets values of human dignity, equality and freedom that apply in every workplace.
  • Law: legislation such as the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 or the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 turns some values into legal duties.
  • The profession: codes of conduct of professional bodies and councils, for example registration requirements for natural scientists or veterinary para-professionals.
  • The organisation: mission statements, codes of conduct and policies of the department, co-operative or company you work for. The public service, for instance, has a code of conduct for its employees.

Ethics

Ethics is the careful thinking about what is right and wrong, and the principles we use to decide. Values tell us what matters; ethics helps us decide what to do when values compete. A practitioner who believes in both helping farmers quickly and following procurement rules faces an ethical question when a farmer begs for seed that has not been approved through the system.

Reflecting on your own values

Being a professional starts with knowing your own values and blind spots. Ask yourself: Which of my values come from my upbringing, and which from my training? Would I be comfortable if my decision were reported in the local newspaper? Do I treat a poor smallholder with the same respect as a large commercial farmer? Honest reflection prepares you for the hard decisions that come later.

lessons.title: Professional accountability and the organisation
lessons.html:
Being accountable

Accountability means being answerable for your decisions, actions and their results, and accepting the consequences. A professional is accountable in several directions at once.

Accountable toExample
Clients and communitiesGiving correct advice on a vaccination programme and following up
EmployerUsing the vehicle, budget and time for official work only
ProfessionStaying within your scope of competence and keeping knowledge current
The lawFollowing legislation on animal welfare, chemicals and natural resources
ColleaguesDoing your share and supporting the team
YourselfActing in line with your conscience

Practising accountability

  • Keep accurate records of advice given, funds used and decisions made.
  • Admit mistakes early and help correct them instead of hiding them.
  • Only give advice within your competence; refer to a vet, soil scientist or engineer when needed.
  • Declare conflicts of interest, for example if a relative applies for project support.
  • Never accept gifts or favours that could influence your decisions.

Values in an organisational context

Organisations state their values in mission statements, codes of conduct and policies, and show their real values in how they reward and discipline people. Professional values fit an organisation well when the organisation supports quality service, fairness and honesty. Problems arise when stated values and actual practice differ, for example when an organisation claims to put farmers first but measures staff only by the number of forms filled in.

Understanding the organisation's structure, chain of command, delegation of authority and grievance and whistle-blowing procedures helps you act on your values in a proper way. In South Africa the Protected Disclosures Act 26 of 2000 protects employees who report wrongdoing through the correct channels in good faith.

lessons.title: Value conflict in the workplace and how to deal with it
lessons.html:
Why value conflicts happen

Value conflicts occur when two or more values, or the values of different people or groups, point to different actions. Common causes in agriculture and extension are:

  • Personal values clash with organisational policy, for example a rule that excludes a struggling farmer from support.
  • Pressure from managers, politicians or community leaders to favour certain people.
  • Competing goals, such as fast service versus proper procedure, or production versus environmental protection.
  • Cultural differences in how decisions should be made, who should speak and how time is treated.
  • Scarce resources: ten groups want the only tractor in the same week.

Case: the borrowed bakkie

A supervisor asks an extension officer to use the government bakkie on Saturday to collect his own furniture, saying everyone does it. The officer values loyalty to the supervisor but also honesty and proper use of public property. This is a conflict between loyalty and integrity, and the law and code of conduct are clear that official vehicles are for official use.

A step-by-step approach

  1. Identify the facts and who is affected.
  2. Name the values in conflict.
  3. Check the rules: law, code of conduct, organisational policy.
  4. Consider options and their consequences for each person.
  5. Test the decision: Is it legal? Is it fair? Would I be comfortable if it were public?
  6. Act and communicate respectfully, for example: I am not able to use the vehicle for private work, but I can help you find a hire bakkie.
  7. Escalate through proper channels if pressure continues, and keep notes.

Ways of handling conflict between people

Where the conflict is between colleagues or groups, use dialogue: listen to each side, look for shared interests (everyone wants the project to succeed), and seek a solution both can accept. Mediation by a neutral person can help. Avoid gossip, ultimatums and silent resentment.

Key points

  • Professional values come from personal background, society, law, the profession and the organisation.
  • Accountability means answering for your actions to clients, employer, profession, the law and yourself.
  • Declare conflicts of interest and never accept gifts that could influence decisions.
  • Value conflicts arise from competing values, pressure, scarce resources and cultural differences.
  • Use a step-by-step approach: facts, values, rules, options, test, act, escalate.

Being answerable for your decisions and actions and their results
Doing what the manager says without question
